'''Cesare Arzelà''' (6 March 1847–15 March 1912) was an Italian [[mathematician]] who taught at the [[University of Bologna]] and is recognized for his contributions in the [[Functions (mathematics)|theory of functions]], particularly for his characterization of [[Sequence (mathematics)|sequences]] of [[continuous function]]s, generalizing the one given earlier by [[Giulio Ascoli]] in the [[Arzelà–Ascoli theorem]].

==Life==
He was a pupil of the [[Scuola Normale Superiore]] of [[Pisa]] where he graduated in 1869. Arzelà came from a poor household; therefore he could not start his study until 1871, when he studied in Pisa under [[Enrico Betti]] and [[Ulisse Dini]].

He was working in [[Florence]] (from 1875) and in 1878 obtained the Chair of Algebra at the [[University of Palermo]].

After that, he became a professor in 1880 at the [[University of Bologna]] at the Department of analysis. He conducted research in the field of [[Functions (mathematics)|theory of functions]]. His most famous student was [[Leonida Tonelli]].

In 1889 he generalized the [[Giulio Ascoli|Ascoli]] theorem to [[Arzelà–Ascoli theorem]], an important [[theorem]] in the theory of functions.

He was a member of the [[Accademia Nazionale dei Lincei]], and of several other academies.
